lesson.title: Class Attributes: Sharing Data Across Every Object
lesson.summary: A class attribute is a variable assigned directly inside the class body, outside any method, so its value is shared by every instance of the class instead of belonging to just one of them.
lesson.body:
Instance attributes, created with self.attribute = value inside a method, give each object its own private copy of a value. Sometimes, though, you want every object built from a class to share exactly the same value, such as a species name that is true for every dog regardless of which particular dog you are looking at. A class attribute does this: it is a variable assignment written directly in the class body, at the same indentation level as the method definitions, not inside any of them.

```python
class Dog:
    species = "Canis familiaris"

    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

rex = Dog("Rex")
fido = Dog("Fido")
print(rex.species, fido.species)
print(Dog.species)

Dog.species = "Canis lupus familiaris"
print(rex.species, fido.species)
```

```
Canis familiaris Canis familiaris
Canis familiaris
Canis lupus familiaris Canis lupus familiaris
```

Neither rex nor fido has its own "species" entry in its instance __dict__, since __init__ never assigns self.species. When you write rex.species, Python looks for "species" on the object first, does not find it, and then falls back to looking on the class itself, where it does find it. That is why updating Dog.species updates what both rex.species and fido.species report, in one shot: there was only ever one "species" value in memory, owned by the class, and every instance was simply reading it.

This sharing is convenient, but it hides a classic trap when the shared class attribute is mutable, like a list, rather than an immutable value like a string.

```python
class Dog:
    tricks = []

    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

    def add_trick(self, trick):
        self.tricks.append(trick)

rex = Dog("Rex")
fido = Dog("Fido")

rex.add_trick("sit")
print(rex.tricks)
print(fido.tricks)
```

```
['sit']
['sit']
```

Even though only rex.add_trick("sit") was called, fido.tricks also shows ['sit']. self.tricks.append(trick) does not create an instance attribute at all: it looks up tricks, finds the single shared list living on the class since self has no tricks of its own, and mutates that one list in place, so the change is visible through every instance, including ones that never called add_trick themselves. This is the classic mutable default class attribute gotcha, and the fix is to give each object its own list as an instance attribute instead, typically by assigning self.tricks = [] inside __init__, so append modifies a list private to that one object rather than one shared by the whole class.
